extracted.intended_audience: IP professionals, patent analysts, in-house and outside counsel, and patent portfolio/standards strategists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing 5G standard-essential patent (SEP) landscape by combining SEP declaration data, worldwide patent records, and standards contributions to assess leadership, essentiality, and strategic portfolio positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEP declaration databases are imperfect starting points
rubrics_metrics.description: SEP declaration databases are meant to document fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory (FRAND) obligations and are not maintained to provide an accurate landscape of verified SEPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declaration practices vary by filer and SSO: some companies declare after careful claim mapping, others declare broadly or using blanket declarations; declarations are often filed while patents are pending and standards still evolve, so many declared patents may ultimately be non-essential or declarations may be incomplete. Use declaration databases as the best publicly available starting point but treat results cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of 'maximal declaration' (over-declaration) phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Some declaration regimes result in many declared patents that cannot be verified as essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example expert reports indicate approximately 10-47% of all ETSI declared 2G/3G/4G patents can be verified as essential (citing Unwired Planet v. Huawei, TCL v. Ericsson). Expect over-declaration in some datasets and adjust analysis/validation accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of 'minimal declaration' (under-declaration) phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Other declaration regimes systematically under-report potentially essential patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: approximately 10-20% of Wi‑Fi SEPs are declared at IEEE (estimates in Microsoft Corp. v. Motorola, Inc.); approximately 20-30% of HEVC SEPs are declared at ITU‑T (comparisons of pooled HEVC SEPs). Where declarations are sparse, many SEPs will be missing from public declaration lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blanket declarations provide no disclosure of SEP magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Some SSOs (e.g., IEEE, ITU) permit 'blanket declarations' where companies do not declare specific patent numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blanket practices mean no transparency about how many or which patents a company claims as potentially essential; these databases cannot be used to infer magnitude of SEP ownership without further investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-correlate declared patents with worldwide patent records and standards databases
rubrics_metrics.description: To identify 5G patents, integrate ETSI declared patents with worldwide patent information and the 3GPP standards database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matching declared patent numbers to patent family data, ownership history and 3GPP/ETSI technical specifications yields richer, actionable insights than raw declaration lists alone (see figure 1 concept in the article).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use TS number and version to classify standard generation and technical locus
rubrics_metrics.description: Declared patents typically provide the relevant technical specification (TS) number and version that the patent is allegedly essential for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TS number and version allow retrieval of: standards generation (2G/3G/4G/5G), standard subgroup (e.g., RAN1, RAN2, SA2, CT1), standard release number (e.g., Release 14/15/16), and standard publication date (helps infer possible product implementation date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extract patent metadata from declared patent numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Declared patent numbers enable pulling patent-level metadata required for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important patent fields include current owner (first applicant and reassignments), status (granted/pending/revoked/active/lapsed/expired), family ID (INPADOC extended/simple family), and dates (priority, filing, grant, expiration). Use these to understand ownership, life-cycle, and enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count declared patent families by declaration year using an INPADOC extended family definition
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing declaration trends, count declared patent families as of the year of declaration using a consistent family definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses INPADOC extended families; declarations can be counted multiple times across generations if the same patent family is declared for 2G/3G/4G/5G at different times (i.e., count per generation when declared for multiple generations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify declarations to generations by cross-correlation and keyword/project description
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign declared patents to 2G/3G/4G/5G by correlating the declared TS with ETSI and 3GPP data and by checking project description keywords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also mark declarations that reference terms like 'LTE', '4G', 'New Radio', or '5G'. Be aware that patents can be essential across multiple generations; use explicit TS mapping where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count standards contributions per company as a proxy for standards leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing the number of contributions submitted per company at consortia (e.g., 3GPP) helps assess involvement and likely future SEP strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributions are a measure of investment and influence: frequent, high-quality contributions build credibility and enable companies to integrate their technologies (sometimes patented) into standards. Use contribution counts as one indicator among others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refine contribution counts by type, category, and status
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all contributions are equal — classify contributions by type (work item, change request, input, output, draft), category (feature addition, correction/editorial, functional modification), and status (agreed, approved, incorporated, noted, rejected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude non-technical categories when using contributions to indicate technical leadership. The type indicates magnitude (e.g., a work item is an initial idea; a change request modifies existing projects) and the status indicates whether the contribution influenced the final spec.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight contribution impact by type and category when assessing influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The type and category of a contribution demonstrates how much it influences the final standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, work items (new specification ideas) generally have greater influence than editorial corrections; a technical addition is more indicative of innovation than an editorial change. Use these differences to prioritize contributions in leadership assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate first contributor from supporting contributors for attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions are often submitted by multiple companies; typically one company is the main contributor and others support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the first contributor as the likely principal technology provider (leader of the pack) and supporting contributors as endorsers who may provide little technical input. This distinction matters when attributing standards influence and likely SEP ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster contributions by generation, working group, and release for technical alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate contributions to specific generations (3G/4G/5G/Wi‑Fi versions), standards groups (RAN1, SA2, TGn, etc.), and releases (Release 12–16 etc.) to understand technical scope and timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clustering helps map contributions to the parts of the standard they affect and to corresponding patent prosecution opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standards contribution analysis to infer likely SEPs when declaration data is incomplete
rubrics_metrics.description: When SEP declaration databases are incomplete (e.g., Wi‑Fi, video codecs), analyzing who submits technical contributions can indicate who will likely own SEPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because contributions show where companies invest technical effort, contribution counting supplements declaration data to reveal likely future SEP owners—useful for markets where declarations under-report SEPs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategically align R&D, standards development, and patent prosecution teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-departmental coordination is required to ensure inventions disclosed by R&D are protected, brought into standards, and prosecuted as SEPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process: R&D invention → decision by patent board to file → preserve priority (e.g., provisional filing) → standards developers introduce the solution as a contribution → patent prosecution team aligns claim language to the evolving standard and verifies novelty/prior art. Organizational alignment increases chances of filing valid and essential SEPs.

rubrics_metrics.name: File early provisional applications to protect contribution-derived inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Early filing protects inventions before contributions are submitted to working groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional filings allow standards developers to disclose and push technology into standards while preserving priority for later patent applications; coordinate filing timing with standards activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align and amend patent claims during prosecution to map to the latest standard version
rubrics_metrics.description: Because standards change iteratively, claim language should be adapted during prosecution to correspond to the final standard implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim amendments can be used up until grant to ensure the granted patent can be charted to the latest standard version—while also ensuring claims remain novel over prior art. Patent prosecution teams must monitor standard evolution and update claims accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage algorithmic techniques to estimate essentiality rates and predict essential patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithmic-based techniques for calculating essentiality rates and predicting patent essentiality can scale analysis and get closer to identifying truly essential SEPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods can reduce the time and resources needed for manual essentiality determination, but should be validated with subject-matter expert input and cross-data checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a combined patent-and-standards-data approach for business-ready insights
rubrics_metrics.description: IP professionals should consider both patent filing data and standardization data to align portfolios and make actionable business decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combined data for licensing, acquisitions, joining patent pools, and competitive analysis. The goal is to convert raw declarations and contributions into strategic, organization-wide decisions and to anticipate overlaps between technologies and IP rights as connectivity expands.
